The concert opens with black-and-white projections of street scenes as Swift rises from beneath the stage to sing "Welcome to New York," followed by "New Romantics" and "Blank Space," and an industrial rock version of "I Knew You Were Trouble." The set moves through "I Wish You Would," a Singin' in the Rain-inspired staging of "How You Get the Girl" with dancers twirling neon umbrellas, and "I Know Places," in which masked dancers chase her through moving doors. Swift introduces "Clean" by sharing lessons from her personal life and performs a synth-driven "Love Story" on an elevated platform that sweeps around the stadium. Later highlights include "Style," "This Love," "Bad Blood" in a black leather suit, a rock rendition of "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" on electric guitar, a piano mashup of "Enchanted" and "Wildest Dreams," and "Out of the Woods" beneath giant paper planes, before the show closes with "Shake It Off" on a platform above the crowd amid fireworks and confetti.

The tour began in Tokyo on 5 May 2015 and ended in Melbourne on 12 December, spanning 85 shows. It was the highest-grossing tour of 2015, selling more than 2.27 million tickets and grossing over 250 million dollars, and critics praised Swift's stage presence and connection with her audience, while her parade of celebrity guests drew wide comment. Announced on 13 December 2015, the film premiered exclusively on Apple Music on 20 December 2015 and remained on the service until 22 May 2020; footage from it was also used in the music video for "New Romantics."

Sailing in the New World, Monkey D. Luffy and the Straw Hat Pirates are challenged by Captain Foxy to a Davy Back Fight rematch. The contest is a trap devised by Kōmei, a brilliant strategist who has recently joined Foxy's crew. During an eating contest, Zoro and Sanji consume a strange mushroom that saps their strength and turns them into good-for-nothings, and the pair are captured and carried away. Chasing their friends, the Straw Hats reach Nebulandia, an island shrouded in a mist formed from sea water that, like seastone, neutralises the powers of Devil Fruit users. Their arrival is exactly what Kōmei planned.

Kōmei is in fact a vice admiral of the Navy and a special operations strategist who infiltrated the Foxy Pirates by deliberately losing to them. Having lost his home town to pirates as a child, he despises them and dreams of proving that ordinary people without powers can defeat Devil Fruit users through cunning, thereby changing the Navy itself. Luffy is forced into an uneasy alliance with his old Davy Back rival Foxy for the rescue. Using the island's terrain and a series of traps, especially the pitfalls he favours, Kōmei captures Robin, Franky and Usopp, but Brook and Chopper, searching for an antidote to the mushroom, foil his attempt to seize Luffy. In the final battle, Kōmei floods his base with sea water to weaken Luffy, but Foxy's Slow-Slow Beam and a pitfall turn the tables, and Luffy defeats him with a decisive blow.

The regular voice cast returns, led by Mayumi Tanaka as Luffy, Kazuya Nakai as Zoro and Hiroaki Hirata as Sanji, with Toshio Shimada as Foxy. Ichikawa Ennosuke voices Kōmei, a role he modelled on the Three Kingdoms strategist Zhuge Liang, while Hoka Kinoshita plays another new crew member who is secretly a Navy officer.

The story revolves around Carlos (played by Karra Elejalde), a former professional soccer player who has lost his passion for the game after a serious injury. He is now working as a coach at a local soccer school in Madrid, where he tries to teach young players the basics of the sport. However, his unorthodox coaching methods and lack of patience with his students make him unpopular among both the kids and their parents.

One day, Carlos receives an offer from a wealthy businessman named Juan (played by Luis Zahera) to coach his daughter, Frida (played by Blanca Suárez), in a series of high-stakes soccer matches. The catch is that Frida has never played soccer before, but she's determined to become the best player in Spain.

As Carlos begins working with Frida, he realizes that she's not just any ordinary student - she's a talented and feisty young woman who refuses to be told what to do. Despite their initial disagreements, Carlos starts to see potential in Frida and decides to help her develop her skills.

Throughout the movie, Carlos and Frida face numerous challenges as they prepare for the big matches. They encounter rival coaches, tough opponents, and even some personal struggles that threaten to derail their partnership. However, with each passing match, Carlos and Frida grow closer, both on and off the field.

As the stakes get higher, Carlos starts to realize that his feelings for Frida go beyond mere coaching. He begins to develop romantic feelings for her, but he's hesitant to express them, fearing it might compromise their professional relationship.

In the end, Carlos and Frida face off against their toughest opponents yet - a team of ruthless and experienced players who will stop at nothing to win. With Carlos' unorthodox tactics and Frida's determination, they manage to pull off an incredible comeback victory.

As the dust settles, Carlos finally confesses his feelings to Frida, and she reveals that she feels the same way. The movie ends with a heartwarming moment of tenderness between the two leads, as they share a kiss on the field.

Overall, No Manches Frida is a fun and entertaining film that explores themes of love, friendship, and perseverance. With its lighthearted tone and engaging storyline, it's a great choice for anyone looking for a feel-good movie experience.

Jason Brady (Werkheiser), a teenager who posts videos of his songs online, is sent by his parents to a Catholic boarding school after wrecking his father's car; they disapprove of his musical ambitions. His studious sister Zoe (Newman) attends the same school. The new teacher, Sister Sophia (Ochse), is welcomed by the headmistress, Sister Rebecca (Eigenberg), but Zoe soon notices that she skips the morning prayer and knows little about the faith. In truth she is Laura, a disturbed woman who became obsessed with Jason through his videos, murdered the real Sister Sophia and took her identity. Under her habit she wears lingerie and makeup; she moves Jason's girlfriend Sara (Avery) away from him in class, threatens her, and lets the boy glimpse her undressing. She plants a joint that gets Sara suspended and hides whiskey in Jason's room so that he must stay at school over a weekend, seduces him and secretly films them together, then frames Zoe for cheating when the girl grows suspicious. After Sara returns, Laura kills her in the shower and stages it as an accident. At a family dinner, Zoe catches the "nun" in lie after lie, and Jason confesses the affair and the sex tape she is using against him. The siblings search her computer, discover her real name and seek out Sister Rebecca, only to find her knocked unconscious. Laura confronts them in the chapel, but Sister Rebecca intervenes and Jason stabs the impostor with a screwdriver.

Reviewers who cover Lifetime films responded warmly to its excesses. Lisa Marie Bowman of Through the Shattered Lens called it an over-the-top masterpiece of the network's style, praising Campbell for playing up the sordid melodrama without taking it too seriously and singling out Ochse's switches between the cheerful nun and the irritated Laura. Lifetime Uncorked gave it a rating of three knives, though it found the casting of a genuinely teenage-looking actor as Jason somewhat creepy.

Barbie and her best friends Renee (Stephanie Sheh) and Teresa (Jenny Pellicer) are gymnasts preparing for a championship, though Barbie is shaken after losing focus during the team's pyramid. Renee's Aunt Zoe (Cathy Weseluck), a cat-loving knitter who never misses a meet, invites the girls to a picnic at the Hollywood sign, where a hidden door leads to the headquarters of a secret spy organisation, the International Intelligence and Innovation Agency. Zoe turns out to be its head, Agent Z. Impressed by the girls' agility and teamwork, she recruits them to stop a cat burglar stealing rare gems which, once assembled, could power a device able to shut down the agency's systems.

Trained by Agent Dunbar (Brian Dobson) and equipped by the young inventor Lazlo (Ian Hanlin) with gadgets disguised as make-up and fashion accessories, motorcycles and a robotic dog named Percy, the girls must keep their mission secret even from their sisters. Their inexperience costs them dearly: the thief, a superb gymnast, escapes with a gem at their first stakeout and again at a party where their kitchen disguises end in chaos, and they are dismissed from the agency. Applying Zoe's advice to visualise a move before making it, Barbie recognises the burglar's moves in their rival gymnast Patricia (Rebecca Husain). Following her into headquarters, the girls discover she has been working for Dunbar, who resents being passed over and plans to use the gems to cripple the agency, frame Zoe and take her place. With help from Zoe, their friends and the agency's robots, the girls foil the scheme, Barbie regains her confidence, and Patricia, realising her mistakes, makes friends with the trio.

The supporting cast includes Alyssya Swales as Barbie's younger sister Chelsea, Elizabeth Irving as Mila and Kathleen Barr as Violet.

Structured as a conversation in which Smith poses questions and Johns explains the characters and their place in the shared universe, the special works through the upcoming releases one by one. It begins with Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice, then due in March 2016, reusing footage from earlier trailers while cast members recall their first encounters with DC comics and Johns outlines why the two heroes come into conflict. It then turns to Suicide Squad and premieres a new trailer for the film set to Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody", before offering the first brief glimpses of footage from Wonder Woman, starring Gal Gadot and scheduled for 2017. The final section introduces the other members of the planned Justice League, Aquaman, the Flash and Cyborg, using concept art and short summaries of their backstories; Johns acknowledges the television version of the Flash while explaining that Ezra Miller's cinematic Barry Allen will have a somewhat different origin. The special's main announcement was that Green Lantern and the Green Lantern Corps would join the film universe, with Hal Jordan and John Stewart expected to be at its center.

Reactions were mixed. Geekscape felt it achieved what it set out to do, bringing viewers up to speed on the characters, and found Smith's enthusiasm infectious, though it noted that the Batman v Superman segment offered little new and that the Wonder Woman footage left it flat. Dan Greenfield of 13th Dimension was far more critical, calling it a half-hour infomercial aimed at viewers who already knew the characters, questioning the need for Smith as a cheerleader and arguing that the studio should show rather than tell, though he preferred the new Suicide Squad trailer to the first.

At Monster High, Lagoona Blue, who grew up in the Great Scarrier Reef, watches her friends Frankie, Draculaura and Clawdeen struggle through dance rehearsals under Toralei's poor coaching, but refuses to join them, though she dances beautifully when she thinks she is alone. At the recital Toralei exposes her dancing behind the curtain, and Lagoona freezes, becomes tangled in the stage rigging and finds the video viral the next day. When she uninvites Toralei from her poolside party, the two quarrel, Toralei falls into the pool, and a whirlpool pulls Lagoona, Toralei, Frankie, Draculaura, Clawdeen and Gil to the bottom of the sea, where they find themselves transformed into half-fish creatures.

Posea Reef, daughter of Poseidon, tends a garden in which every plant represents a sea creature; Lagoona's is wilting, and Posea tells her that to go home she must face her greatest fear. Lagoona reveals that her stage fright dates from a childhood dance competition in which her former friend Kala, a squid ghoul, deliberately tripped her. Staying with Lagoona's father and siblings, the group learns that a feared Kraken has been sighted. Kala challenges Lagoona to a dance-off, and through the serpent sisters Peri and Pearl tricks her with a false legend that looking the Kraken in the eye cures fear. Lagoona braves its lair but faints on stage again; when her friends rally the crowd to support her, a furious Kala summons the Kraken, which follows the friends back to Monster High. Climbing onto the monster, Lagoona realises her true fear was Kala's bullying, while Kala admits she was mocked for her looks and that the Kraken is her father, whom she was ashamed of. The two reconcile, the Kraken helps repair the school, and both girls' plants return to health.

Larissa Gallagher voices Lagoona, with Kate Higgins as Frankie, Debi Derryberry as Draculaura, Salli Saffioti as Clawdeen, America Young as Toralei, Lyndsy Kail as Kala and Paula Rhodes as Posea.

Set in 1958 in an unnamed country, the story takes place at a strict, isolated boarding school deep in a forest. Alex, a troubled boy sent there after a prank that ended in tragedy, upsets the institution's rigid discipline from the moment he arrives. He bonds with three fellow students who share a single goal, to escape, and, inspired by legends of former pupils who supposedly managed to flee, the four friends begin plotting a breakout. Alex also falls for Daniela, one of the girls boarding at the school. As the friends defy the adults' authority and abuse, their flirtations and escape attempts begin to uncover the school's dark secrets, and the friendship and loyalty among them become essential for surviving an atmosphere ruled by fear and humiliation. The title's "wolf", the predator destroying the lives of those who cross its path, ultimately proves to be the school's own director, played by García Lozano.

The film addresses abuse committed in the name of education and good behaviour, violence, freedom and the anxieties of adolescence, mixing suspense with touches of comedy and romance; its message is that the living can be more frightening than the dead. It was shot across eighteen locations that together form the boarding school, conceived almost as a character in its own right.

Critics praised the period atmosphere, art direction and cinematography but were divided on the rest. Time Out México gave it three stars out of five, describing a film with a distinct personality within contemporary Mexican cinema and noting influences ranging from Carlos Enrique Taboada's Hasta el viento tiene miedo to the Harry Potter stories. CineNT found it predictable and overlong, with stilted dialogue and uneven child performances, though it singled out García Lozano's frighteningly human headmaster, and El Blog de Yes considered it a disappointing coming-of-age thriller hampered by a flat script and tedious pacing.

The documentary follows the creative process from character conception to animation. It accompanies the team on a research trip to Kenya, where they study animals in their natural habitats, and examines the artwork produced for the film, from sketches of its expressive animal characters to its highly detailed environments. The filmmakers explain the film's roots in their love of Disney films in which animals walk upright and wear clothes, such as the studio's 1973 version of Robin Hood. Rather than cataloguing every aspect of production, however, most of the film concentrates on the evolution of the story, which changed dramatically during development. In early versions, the con artist fox Nick Wilde was the protagonist instead of the rabbit police officer Judy Hopps, and the fragile peace between predators and prey was maintained only because the predators were forced to wear shock collars. The documentary traces in depth how the storytellers moved from that version to the finished film, and how they approached the real-world themes of prejudice and bias in what is essentially a family film.

The film follows DiCaprio, appointed a United Nations Messenger of Peace on climate change in 2014, on a three-year journey around the world to document the impact of global warming. He travels by snowmobile along the coast of Greenland, where melting ice is turning the region from a reflector of sunlight into an absorber of heat, flies over the Canadian oil sands, visits Miami Beach as it raises its streets against rising seas, and sees the burning rainforests of Sumatra cleared for palm oil plantations. In India he visits flood-ravaged farmland, in Kiribati he sees communities already displaced by flooding, and at NASA he studies ocean models with astronaut and scientist Piers Sellers, who was then living with terminal cancer. He meets Barack Obama, Pope Francis, Ban Ki-moon, John Kerry and Elon Musk, whom he joins at the Tesla Gigafactory, as well as Sunita Narain and scientists including Johan Rockström and Michael E. Mann.

DiCaprio uses Hieronymus Bosch's triptych The Garden of Earthly Delights, a reproduction of which hung above his crib as a child, as an analogy for humanity's path toward ruin, and the film also draws on the production of his film The Revenant. It devotes particular attention to climate change denial among American politicians and lobbyists, and argues for a carbon tax to shift investment to renewable energy; the production offset its own emissions through a voluntary carbon tax.

The story is set in the Arizona Territory in the 1870s. Introduced by his own narration as he rides through the desert, Marshal Wilcox has captured the outlaw George Rivers and is escorting him to the frontier town of Crumpit to face justice, fighting off a gang of bandits along the way. In Crumpit, however, an innocent man condemned to hang has placed a curse on the town, and the dead begin rising from their graves with a hunger for living flesh. On the trail Wilcox meets Sergeant Bale, a Buffalo Soldier of the U.S. Army, and the travelers rescue and befriend an Apache who joins them. Meanwhile, in town, a small group of survivors, among them a pair of young people, an elderly preacher and Jasper, a barman of short stature, barricade themselves inside the saloon while the undead roam the streets outside and plan their escape. When the marshal's party reaches Crumpit and discovers that it too has been overrun, they join forces with the survivors, and the lawman, the soldier, the Apache and the outlaw prisoner must learn to survive together as they try to fight their way to freedom, with a siege in the saloon and a railway handcar among the film's set pieces.

The film was released on DVD in the United Kingdom by Left Films in August 2016 and in the United States by Wild Eye Releasing, and reviews were negative. Joel Harley of Horror DNA called it dull and bland, criticizing its sets, unconvincing actors, unimaginative story and some of the cheapest zombies seen in a no-budget horror film, though he credited it with more ambition than it might have had in letting its characters travel beyond the town. Daniel Goodwin of Scream magazine faulted its amateur acting, cut-rate effects and dithering narrative, while Horror Society, rating it two out of five, found most of the cast convincing but judged Winters unpersuasive as the marshal and the story thin and unexplained.

Draculaura, the daughter of Count Dracula, has spent her life in her father's mansion, forbidden to mingle with humans and dreaming of friends and a normal life. One night Frankie Stein, daughter of Frankenstein's creature, knocks at the door, having seen Draculaura turn into a bat. The two decide to open a school for monsters, who have always lived in hiding, even from one another. In the forest they recruit the werewolf Clawdeen Wolf, whose mother and brothers move in, and the mansion is converted into Monster High. Draculaura's blog, posted on the secret Monster Internet, draws thousands of followers, and with a magical amulet that teleports them to any monster whose name they know, the ghouls travel the world, recruiting the mummy Cleo de Nile in Egypt, Lagoona Blue in Australia, Deuce Gorgon and Venus McFlytrap.

Draculaura and Frankie run for student council presidents, promising a world where humans and monsters can coexist and rashly vowing to bring Draculaura's favourite pop star, Tash, to the school dance. Their rival is Moanica D'Kay, a zombie who commands an army of "Zomboyz" and wants monsters to rule over humans. She mocks the girls' dream, and Tash rejects Draculaura in horror at the sight of her fangs. Draculaura and Frankie nonetheless win the election, but Moanica crashes the dance with Tash as her hostage, planning to turn her into a zombie. Draculaura defeats Moanica in bat form, and when Moanica lunges at the singer and passes straight through her, Tash reveals that she is in fact a ghost named Ari Hauntington, who had disguised herself to live among humans, and she finally accepts being a monster.

The voice cast includes Debi Derryberry as Draculaura, Cassandra Lee Morris as Frankie, Salli Saffioti as Clawdeen and Cleo, Cristina Milizia as Moanica, Michael Sorich as Dracula and Jonquil Goode as Tash.

In Paris in 1967, Godard, the celebrated 37-year-old figurehead of the French New Wave, falls in love with the 20-year-old Anne while directing her in La Chinoise, and asks her to marry him on the day the radio reports news of the submarine Le Redoutable. His growing commitment to Maoism shapes his work, but the film is rejected by the Chinese embassy and poorly received by critics and audiences. A year later the events of May 1968 erupt. Godard joins the often violent street protests, is pestered by fans who want him to return to lighter films such as Breathless and Pierrot le Fou, is shouted down at the occupied Sorbonne and mocked in graffiti, and meets the same scorn at a conference in Rome hosted by Bertolucci. He and friends travel to the Cannes Film Festival, which they help shut down in solidarity with the strikes, and then find themselves stranded without fuel during the general strike.

Back in Paris, Godard founds the Dziga Vertov Group with Jean-Pierre Gorin to make radical political cinema, but he becomes increasingly isolated, accused by others of being incomprehensible. As Anne pursues her own acting career, their marriage deteriorates and Godard attempts suicide with an overdose. Anne falls out of love, and they separate during the collective shoot of Wind from the East, where Godard is confronted with his own contradictions.

The story opens with park owner Simon Masrani flying Claire Dearing to the island and showing off with aerial stunts, until he crashes into the aviary and tumbles out of his helicopter. Owen Grady rescues him with the help of a trained Pteranodon. Before he is driven away in an ambulance, Masrani tells Claire that Jurassic World will need a new attraction. Meanwhile, the security chief Vic Hoskins goes hunting in the woods and mistakes a park employee in a dinosaur costume for the real thing, chasing him through the jungle for much of the film.

Claire resolves to create a brand-new dinosaur. Owen doubts it can be done, but Dr. Henry Wu proves otherwise by combining Velociraptor and Carnotaurus DNA, and Owen later discovers a whole collection of earlier hybrids kept in an old section of the island. Wu's newest creation, the Indominus rex, turns out to have an insatiable appetite for hot dogs. When it spots the same costumed employee, now dressed as a hot dog mascot, it breaks out of its enclosure and pursues him. Claire calls in the containment unit, rams the beast with a truck and uses a trail of hot dogs to lure it, while Owen's raptors briefly turn against the soldiers because the Indominus shares their DNA. Eventually Owen arrives with the old Tyrannosaurus and the hybrids, and together they drive the Indominus into a pit. The next day visitors enjoy the new attraction, dinosaurs kicking a gyrosphere like a ball with Hoskins still trapped inside, while in a closing scene Wu feeds a second Indominus.
